paras: The lynching of Levi Harrington took place in Kansas City, Missouri, on the night of April 3, 1882, when a mob took Harrington, a young Black man, from police officers and hanged him from the Bluff street bridge. He had been arrested on suspicion after the fatal shooting of police officer Pat Jones, and newspapers soon reported that he was probably innocent. A criminal-court judge directed a grand jury to indict the lynchers for murder, and an alleged mob leader was tried in December 1882, ending in a hung jury.

Jones, an officer of the Metropolitan police force, had just reached home on the evening of Monday, April 3, when a nearby storekeeper pointed out two Black men carrying goods he believed were stolen. The wire reports differed on the goods: the Associated Press said butter, while the National Associated Press said articles taken from a freight car. When Jones approached, one of the men fired three shots and killed him, and both men ran.

According to the Sedalia Bazoo, the shooter and his companion escaped, and Harrington was arrested later and taken to the police station. The Associated Press dispatch said instead that one of the two men was seized and held by bystanders until police took him to the West Kansas City station. A crowd gathered at police headquarters and demanded the prisoner, and when officers refused and tried to move him to the central station or another secure place, the mob overpowered them.

The crowd, crying "Hang him," carried Harrington to the Bluff street bridge, a bridge "in the heart of the city," and hanged him while he protested his innocence. Shots were then fired into the hanging body, which was later cut down and taken to an undertaker. Later dispatches put the mob at "a thousand men" or at 100.

No arrests were reported in the first days, and the coverage contains no report of an inquest. By mid-April a Black man named Grant was held as an accessory to the policeman's murder, belief was growing that Harrington had been innocent, and a fund was being raised for Jones's widow and five children.

On May 22 Judge White opened the criminal court with a charge calling the grand jury's attention to the murder of "John Harrington, colored," and warned the jurors not to be appalled by the number of murderers they might have to indict. Within days Geo. (or Gus) Miller and Matthew B. Jones were arrested on charges of inciting the mob. In December the Sacramento Record-Union reported that M. V. Jones, described as the mob's leader, had been indicted for murder and that his trial had ended with the jury unable to agree; no later result was found.

The story first spread through two wire services on April 4, appearing in Washington, Alexandria, Omaha and Western papers under headlines such as "An Officer Shot and a Negro Lynched" and "LYNCHED BY A MOB." These dispatches led with the officer's death and referred to the victim only as "the negro," though the National Associated Press version already noted that people generally believed the lynched man innocent. Short items in Kansas, Arizona and South Carolina papers repeated the outline that a man who shot a policeman had been hanged by a mob.

Missouri papers split in tone: the Kirksville Weekly Graphic named "Dick Harrington" as the killer and called him "the struggling wretch," while the Sedalia Bazoo found "no proof against Harrington" and closed, "And such is mob law." Later editorials used the case against lynching generally: the Cairo Bulletin wrote that Kansas City "was disgraced by a lynching," and the Emporia Weekly News recalled the Kansas City prisoner who proved innocent after the mob had killed him. A Seattle grand-jury address listed "Kansas City, Kansas" among recent lynchings, and the Sacramento Record-Union used the Jones trial to decry the belief that an execution by a mob is not murder.

The papers gave the victim's first name as Levi, Dick and John, and the first wires called him "name unknown." Only the Kirksville Weekly Graphic among the fuller accounts said that the lynched man had fired the shots; the Sedalia Bazoo, the court dispatch on "supposed complicity" and later editorials described him as a suspect who was probably innocent. Accounts also placed the shooting on St. Louis avenue or at Jones's own gate, and one reprint misdated the lynching to April 30.

reader.title: Lynching of Levi Harrington
bases: A crowd took a Black prisoner from police and hanged him from a city bridge for the suspected shooting of an officer (A2, A3, A14).

A mob described as large (a 'crowd of a thousand' or 'a mob of 100') took Harrington from officers and hanged him for the suspected killing of Officer Jones (A3, A14, A20, A22); a judge called it murder and one alleged leader was tried for murder (A19, A29).

The Associated Press wire, the National Associated Press wire, the Sedalia Bazoo and later Kansas City court dispatches agree that a Black prisoner was taken from police and hanged from a bridge on the night of April 3 (A2, A3, A14, A19, A20).

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Jones tried to arrest two men suspected of stealing butter and was shot while walking with them; one was held by bystanders, taken to the West Kansas City station, and seized by a mob while being moved to the central station and hanged from Bluff street bridge.

accounts.label: National Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: A grocer pointed out two men carrying goods supposedly from a freight car; a man arrested on suspicion was defended by police against a mob, but a man 'name unknown' was afterward hanged from a bridge, and people generally believed him innocent.

accounts.label: Kirksville Weekly Graphic
accounts.gist: Dick Harrington shot Jones on St. Louis avenue, was overtaken, and was taken from officers by a crowd crying 'Hang him' and hanged despite protesting his innocence.

accounts.label: Sedalia Weekly Bazoo
accounts.gist: The shooter and companion escaped; Levi Harrington was arrested later, the crowd demanded him at police headquarters, and seized him during his removal; there was 'no proof against Harrington'.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'An Officer Shot and a Negro Lynched' and 'LYNCHED BY A MOB' put the officer's killing first and called the victim 'the negro'.
The Kirksville Weekly Graphic headlined 'His Murderer Lynch[ed]', called him 'the struggling wretch' and treated the crowd's 'indignation' as natural.
The Sedalia Bazoo ended 'And such is mob law', saying Harrington was probably 'totally innocent'.
The Cairo Bulletin said Kansas City 'was disgraced by a lynching' and commended Judge White; the Sacramento Record-Union decried a 'lingering barbarism' that held a mob execution was not murder.
